eav.value: a written, risk-based CIP that sits inside the bank's anti-money laundering (AML) program and reflects the methods of opening accounts the bank offers
identity is verified within a reasonable time before or after the account is opened, to the extent reasonable and practicable
eav.source: 31 CFR 1020.220(a)(2)(ii) via the eCFR URL above. VERIFY: wording seen only in secondary summaries this run; if the eCFR text differs, use its exact wording or drop the 'after' half.

eav.value: documentary (an unexpired government photo ID) and non-documentary (checking data against a consumer reporting agency or public database), chosen by the bank's risk-based procedures
eav.source: 31 CFR 1020.220(a)(2)(ii)(A)–(B) via eCFR. VERIFY wording; the 2002 proposed rule (fincen.gov) confirms non-documentary methods for accounts opened online.

eav.value: customers must be able to view a notice of the identification requirements before opening an account; the rule offers sample text headed 'Important Information About Procedures for Opening a New Account', and a website notice or application language qualifies
the FFIEC BSA/AML Examination Manual's CIP section (updated February 2021) tells examiners how to assess a bank's CIP; the manual instructs examiners and does not itself set requirements
Truth in Savings account disclosures go to the customer before the account is opened or a service is provided, whichever is earlier; for an account opened online they must be delivered before opening
Regulation DD disclosures may be delivered electronically subject to the E-SIGN Act's consumer consent provisions (15 U.S.C. 7001 et seq.)

OFAC's Sanctions List Search uses fuzzy name matching with a confidence slider, and OFAC gives no recommended threshold; the free tool is for individual lookups, not automated screening, and does not replace due diligence

for legal entity customers, banks identify and verify beneficial owners under the CDD rule (31 CFR 1010.230); since FinCEN's order of February 13, 2026 (FIN-2026-R001) this is required only when the entity first opens an account, when facts call earlier information into question, or as the bank's risk-based ongoing due diligence requires
NIST SP 800-63-4, final in July 2025, supersedes SP 800-63-3 and splits into 63-4, 63A-4 (identity proofing and enrollment), 63B-4 (authentication) and 63C-4 (federation)
IAL2 identity proofing can be performed remotely or on-site; 'remote unattended' proofing is fully automated with no proofing agent, on devices the provider does not control
eav.source: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63a/introduction ; https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63a/proofing/ . NIST guidance is written for federal agencies; present it as the reference model banks and vendors cite, not as a bank rule.

serpGaps: Every ranking chart draws only the check lane (collect → validate → screen → risk-score → approve/escalate: seon, idenfy, zyphe, mozn, oracle). None draws the screens the customer sees above each check. Our signature visual is a two-lane swimlane: screens on top, checks below.

Wait and failure states are missing: no ranking page designs the pending state, the step-up request, the retry after a blurry ID, or the decline screen. We give each of the 4 outcomes its headline, next action and timing source.

US frame is thin or absent: the vendor guides are global (EU/UK AMLD, generic 'jurisdiction varies'). We tie each step to the US rule that creates it: CIP's four data points and notice (31 CFR 1020.220), Regulation DD disclosure timing and E-SIGN consent, OFAC screening, the CDD beneficial-owner rule and FinCEN's February 13, 2026 relief, NIST SP 800-63A-4.
No page says who owns what: we split decisions between compliance/partner bank, identity vendor and design, which is the honest scope of a design engagement.
Back-office charts (slideteam, process.st, coordinatehq, rocketlane) end at 'account created'. Our chart ends at the first funded account, the fintech activation event.

Business accounts are lumped in with consumers. We give the client onboarding KYC process flow for a legal entity its own section with the 2026 beneficial-owner relief as a concrete UX change (do not re-ask owners when an existing business opens a second account, if compliance confirms).
Accessibility is absent from every ranking page: save-and-resume under WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.7, a non-camera alternative path for document capture, and accessible login under SC 3.3.8.
Measurement stops at 'reduce abandonment' with vendor statistics. We name the events to log per step (no invented benchmarks).

contentModules.title: Onboarding KYC process flow: a flow chart for digital account opening
contentModules.subtitle: The 9 steps from sign-up to a funded account, drawn as two lanes: the screens your customer sees and the checks your bank or partner bank runs, with the waiting, retry, review and decline states most charts leave out.

Second and third sentences translate one US rule into interface: the CIP's four data points become four fields, one notice and at least one wait the customer can see. One sentence on why it matters for a product team (FDIC 48.3% of banked households bank on mobile first). One sentence scoping the post: this is the customer side; compliance owns the rules. First UP link to the hub inside the first 300 words (anchor 'SaaS onboarding design'). No blockquote, no hypothetical-company story in the intro, no question opener, no definition sentence as the first line.

outline.h2: How does an onboarding KYC process flow run, end to end?
outline.answerHint: **An onboarding KYC process flow runs in 9 steps, from the first screen to a funded account: notice and eligibility, contact and consent, identity details, document and selfie capture, automated checks, an outcome, credentials, funding and ongoing monitoring.** (Chart-first H2; not a definition.)
points: One sentence introduces the KYC onboarding process flow chart below (secondary carrier), then the swimlane image (visual 1) + astext ol of the 9 steps with lane labels.
Explain the two lanes in 2–3 sentences: every check in the bottom lane needs a visible state in the top lane.
Name the finish line: first funded account (eav 'finish line'); approval alone is not first value.
Map the PAA '5 stages' question here in one sentence (apply, verify, decide, open, fund) as a reading aid; do not adopt any vendor's 5-stage model.
Bridge: 'The first four steps are where the customer types; start with what the rules ask for.'

outline.h2: Which details does the KYC process flow collect, and in what order?
outline.answerHint: **A US KYC process flow collects at least name, date of birth, address and an identification number such as a Social Security number, and I order the screens easy first and ID document last.**
points: CIP four data points (eav 1) and that the bank's written, risk-based CIP decides the rest (eav 2). 'bank customer onboarding process flow' carrier sentence here.
Field → rule → reason card (visual 2 + astext table).
CIP notice before opening (eav 5): design it as a short, readable screen or an inline line on the application, not a buried link.
Regulation DD disclosures before opening and E-SIGN consent for electronic delivery (eav 7–8): place consent before the first disclosure is sent.

Easy-first order and save-and-resume (eav 'our field order'); WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.7 Redundant Entry for a resumed application (eav 14). Note the security exception (the SSN field may be masked and not re-shown).
Expand abbreviations on first use: Customer Identification Program (CIP), Social Security number (SSN), taxpayer identification number (TIN).
Bridge: 'Typed data is the cheap part. The camera step is where most products lose people (say it as method, not as a statistic).'

outline.h2: Where do document capture and the selfie check fit in the KYC flow?
outline.answerHint: **Document capture and a selfie or liveness check come after the typed details, and only when the bank's risk rules or the identity vendor ask for them; the CIP rule itself allows documentary and non-documentary verification.**
points: Documentary vs non-documentary verification (eav 4; VERIFY wording).
NIST SP 800-63-4 final July 2025, 63A-4 covers identity proofing; IAL2 can be remote; 'remote unattended' defined (eav 11–12). Present NIST as the reference model, not a bank mandate.
Forged media and injection attacks in Revision 4 (eav 13): why vendors add liveness, and why the UI should explain the selfie in one line.
Annotated capture screen (visual 3 + astext).
Accessibility: a path for users without a working camera or who cannot pass a face match; who decides that path (compliance/vendor), what design shows.
Screens follow the vendor SDK; we don't pick the vendor (eav 'ownership split').
Bridge: 'Once the data and images are in, the checks run, and the flow splits.'

outline.h2: How should the onboarding KYC process flow branch after the checks?
outline.answerHint: **After the automated checks, the onboarding KYC process flow splits into four outcomes, approved, step-up, manual review or declined, and each outcome needs its own screen with one next action.**
points: What runs in the check lane: identity verification against data sources, sanctions screening, fraud signals; enhanced due diligence (EDD) for higher risk. Keep it short; the rules are the bank's.
OFAC fuzzy matching and confidence threshold (eav 9): a near match is why a sanctions check can send a legitimate customer to review; the threshold is compliance's decision, never the designer's.
Outcome map (visual 4 + astext table).
Decline copy: what the customer can do next (contact route, adverse-action or other required notices decided by counsel; no legal claims in the post).
LEAD ANGLE 1 at the end of this section (see leadAngle).
Bridge: 'Manual review is the outcome most products leave as a blank screen.'

outline.h2: What should the customer see while KYC review is pending?
outline.answerHint: **While KYC review is pending, the customer should see what is being checked, how long it usually takes from your own data, what happens next and how they will hear back, and nothing they already entered should be lost.**
points: Verification timing under CIP: within a reasonable time before or after opening (eav 3, VERIFY). Design consequence: some programs open a limited account first; that is a compliance decision; the UI must show the limits plainly if they do.
Status tracker states as a text table with placeholder timings ('[your median review time]'); no invented durations.
Notifications: email/SMS/push when status changes; one sentence linking the sibling post on automated onboarding emails and when a person takes over (sideways link).
After approval: credentials (passkeys as syncable authenticators per NIST rev. 4, eav 13) and accessible login (SC 3.3.8, link the fintech page), then the funding screen as the last step.
Bridge: 'All of this is invisible on the chart most banks already have.'

outline.h2: What does a banking client onboarding process flow chart leave out?
outline.answerHint: **A banking client onboarding process flow chart usually maps the bank's checks, approvals and systems, and leaves out the customer's screens, wait states, exits, re-entry points and the events a product team measures.**
points: Ops chart vs product chart split (visual 5 + astext table).
Why both are needed: operations and compliance own the bottom lane; product owns the top lane; disagreements show up where the lanes meet.
'digital customer onboarding' used once as the umbrella term (lexical; no volume claim).
One sentence: back-office templates end at 'account created'; ours ends at the funded account.
Bridge: 'Business accounts add a second person to verify, sometimes several.'

outline.h2: How does the client onboarding KYC process flow change for business accounts?
outline.answerHint: **The client onboarding KYC process flow for a business adds the legal entity's details and its beneficial owners, and since February 13, 2026 FinCEN lets banks skip re-verifying owners each time an existing business customer opens another account, unless facts or the bank's risk procedures call for it.**
points: CDD rule: beneficial owners of legal entity customers (eav 10).

FinCEN order FIN-2026-R001 (eav 10): three circumstances. Design consequence: a returning business opening a second account can confirm existing owner data instead of retyping it, if the bank adopts the relief; the bank decides.
Beneficial owner form patterns: add-another-owner list, invite an owner to complete their own identity step, show who is still pending.
Hyponym H3s allowed: 'Consumer account' vs 'Business account (KYB)'.
Bridge: 'Whatever the account type, you'll only know the flow works if you log each step.'

outline.h2: How do you measure where customers drop out of the KYC flow?
outline.answerHint: **Measure the KYC flow by logging one event per step and tracking step completion, ID retry rate, manual review rate, time in pending and time to funded account, before and after each change.**
points: Event-to-metric list (text table, no benchmark values).
Activation event for a money product = first funded account; sideways link to /blog/saas-onboarding/#where-does-saas-onboarding-end for how to choose an activation event.
Hub measurement facts only: activation rate, time to first value, before and after (hub FAQ). Do not quote vendor abandonment statistics (see notes DO NOT USE).
Bridge: 'Numbers tell you where; the compliance review tells you what you're allowed to change.'

outline.h2: How do you turn the flow chart into screens your compliance team signs off?

faqs.q: What are the steps involved in the bank client onboarding process?
faqs.a: Nine steps on the KYC onboarding process flow chart: notice and eligibility, contact and e-disclosure consent, identity details, document and selfie capture (when required), automated checks, an outcome, credentials, funding and ongoing monitoring. Banks group them differently; the order of data, checks and outcome stays the same.

faqs.q: What is the difference between KYC and CIP?
faqs.a: KYC is the umbrella practice of knowing who a customer is and what risk they bring; the Customer Identification Program is the specific US rule (31 CFR 1020.220) for collecting and verifying identity at account opening. Customer due diligence and enhanced due diligence continue after it.

faqs.q: Does a KYC flow need a selfie or liveness check?
faqs.a: No, not by the CIP rule itself, which allows documentary and non-documentary verification. Many banks and identity vendors add a selfie or liveness step on risk grounds; that is the compliance team's call, and the design should explain the step in one line and offer an alternative path.

faqs.q: Can customers save a KYC application and finish it later?
faqs.a: Yes, and they should be able to. Keep the data they entered (WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.7 Redundant Entry), re-ask only what security requires, such as a masked Social Security number, and tell them where to resume.

faqs.q: Who decides the KYC rules, the designer or the compliance team?
faqs.a: The compliance team, BSA officer and partner bank decide the rules, thresholds and notices; the identity vendor supplies the capture and checks; the designer decides order, copy, states and accessibility. Our designs go to compliance review in annotated files; we do not give legal advice.
